tagline: Two lanes through rolling farmland, with an iron furnace along the way
intro: The Lebanon Cornwall Scenic Byway follows PA 419 from Quentin to the Berks County line, passing rolling farmland and Amish communities. It is a two-lane, undivided road through rural country, with farmland and woodland giving way to residential streets in its towns. VisitPA highlights Cornwall Iron Furnace and the corridor’s farmland among its scenic attractions. PennDOT also records a prohibition on off-premise signs, enforced through local ordinances along this designated stretch.

The road between Cornwall and Schaefferstown was paved by 1930, before the present route number linked these communities. The Quentin-to-Cornwall stretch once carried US 322. That highway moved onto a bypass in 1963; by 1966, PA 419 had been designated along its present alignment. PennDOT records 2008 as the effective year of the Lebanon Cornwall Byway designation, covering the road from PA 72 at Quentin to the county line.

Begin at Quentin and head east through Cornwall on Freeman Drive. After crossing the Lebanon Valley Rail Trail, the road turns northeast and becomes Schaeffer Road through agricultural country. In Schaefferstown, it shares Heidelberg Avenue with PA 897, then turns north on North Market Street. Beyond town, the route curves through farmland to Millbach and Newmanstown’s Main Street before reaching Berks County.

moments.title: Quentin
moments.text: Quentin’s name commemorates a young fighter pilot killed in the First World War. Until October 1920, the village was Bismark, a local spelling of Otto von Bismarck’s name. The new name honored Quentin Roosevelt, President Theodore Roosevelt’s youngest son. PA 419 passes through the community’s center, while PA 72 runs through its eastern side. Their intersection marks the start of the designated byway; Cornwall borders Quentin to the east.

moments.title: Cornwall Iron Furnace
moments.text: At Cornwall, iron ore lay at or close to the surface, with timber, limestone and running water available for smelting. Peter Grubb established the furnace in 1742. The works depended on free laborers, indentured servants and enslaved people. Workers hauled charcoal under a protective roof to keep it dry and dug channels in casting sand to receive the molten iron. A steam engine replaced the waterwheel in 1841, and the furnace stack was rebuilt in the 1850s. Production ended in 1883. The preserved furnace and support buildings now form a historical site and museum, making the scale of the operation legible beyond the furnace itself.

moments.title: Schaefferstown
moments.text: Schaefferstown contains the Gemberling-Rex House, built by Pennsylvania German settlers in 1729 and later altered from its original three-room form. Water still reaches Schaefferstown households through the system Alexander Schaeffer constructed between 1744 and 1750. Located in what is now Fountain Park, it carries water by gravity through underground pipes. The original system supplied two wooden troughs on the square at Main and Market streets. Matilda Zimmerman later replaced one trough in memory of her mother, Mary Rex Zimmerman, a great-granddaughter of Schaeffer. That replacement stands on the south face of the historic bank in the square.
